findings.description: The inline user policy grants full wildcard actions on four powerful services (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) against Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's access key yields the ability to read/delete all S3 data, launch or terminate any EC2 instance, and create/modify Lambda functions — a direct privilege-escalation and data-exfiltration path (e.g. lambda:CreateFunction plus ec2 access can be chained to broaden access).

No pgp_key is supplied, so AWS returns the secret access key in cleartext and Terraform persists it (attribute `secret`) unencrypted in the state file; `encrypted_secret` will be empty. Anyone with read access to the state backend obtains long-lived credentials for a user holding near-administrative permissions.

A permanent programmatic access key is created for an IAM user rather than using short-lived STS role credentials, and there is no rotation mechanism or MFA requirement. Static keys attached to a wildcard policy are a high-value, non-expiring credential for an attacker.

The access key secret is exported as a module output without `sensitive = true`, so it is printed to the console and stored in plaintext in the state/plan artefacts, leaking the credential to CI logs and anyone reading Terraform output.
